units: the writer answers a question his correspondent had asked earlier
two stringed instruments stand in a place where such things are made
on the first, the sound starts when a finger pulls the string aside and lets it go
on the second, a bow drawn across the string brings the sound to life
the tone of the first begins fading the moment it appears
the tone of the second can be held for as long as the movement lasts
the first allows several strings to sound together
the second rarely manages more than two strings at once
the writer recommends the first for backing a singer
text: You asked me to explain how the two instruments standing in the workshop differ, so here is the answer at last. On the first, the sound comes from a finger: it pulls the string aside, then lets go, and the vibration starts with a dry snap. On the second, a bow is drawn across the string, so the tone builds gently and goes on lasting as long as the arm keeps moving. The real gap lies in the way a note begins. Pluck the first, and the note starts fading the very moment it appears. Bow the second, and you can hold the note, swell it, and cut it off exactly when you choose. There is another difference worth knowing about. The first takes several strings at once, so a whole chord sits under the hand, while the second rarely manages more than two. Backing a singer? Choose the first. Shaping one long line? Take the other.

units: the text sorts noise into three categories
the first category covers sounds that never break off
the ear stops noticing these continuous sounds
the second category gathers sounds that return at intervals
the third category concerns very short and violent impacts
an impact of that kind can damage hearing in a moment
how long the exposure lasts counts as much as how loud the sound is
three protections are named: moving away, putting up a barrier, cutting the exposure short
the hearing cells that are destroyed never grow back
text: What exactly counts as noise? The answer splits the field into three families. The first covers continuous sound, the hum of a machine among it, which the ear gradually stops registering. The second gathers intermittent sound, a chiming alarm and its like, forever announcing itself again. The third holds brief, violent impacts, able to wreck hearing in a moment. Is the racket of a building site more to be feared than the murmur of a busy road? Specialists reply that how long you are exposed weighs as much as how loud the source is. What protection is there? Three measures are advised: move away from the source, put an absorbing partition in between, cut the listening short. Can damaged hearing be repaired? The cells that die never grow back, so prevention remains the only route.

units: a learner recounts aloud a lesson he has been given
the specialist asks him to listen in silence to a key being struck
at first the learner hears only one sound
several strings in fact belong to a single key
the specialist deliberately slackens one of the strings
the learner then hears a steady pulsing
doing away with that pulsing is the aim of the operation
the specialist sounds a run of neighbouring notes
the learner tightens the moving part too far during his own attempt
by the end, two strings no longer produce any pulsing
text: The pupil talked his way through the lesson aloud, following the order in which it had happened. The tuner had begun by asking him to listen without speaking while she struck a single key. He answered that he could hear only one note. She pressed the point: three strings sit behind that key. Then she slackened one of them on purpose, and the pupil said a slow beating had come up, like a wave rising and falling back. Tuning, she explained, means getting rid of that beat. After that she played a whole run of neighbouring notes so he could hear them. At last she handed him the lever and let him turn the tuning pin. He tightened too hard, the beating quickened, and she told him to work with a lighter touch. By the end of the lesson, two strings had fallen silent for each other.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: older rooms were low and hung with cloth
sound died away quickly in them
that quick fading allowed fast successions of notes
taller stone halls were built afterwards
sound lingered there long after it had been made
fast passages turned muddy in such halls
those who wrote music then spaced their notes out and made them longer
adding padded seats and audiences cut the lingering down
musical writing grew quicker again after that
the text concludes that materials shaped music as much as taste did
text: Look at what happens to a piece of music when the room around it changes size. Rooms used to be low and hung about with cloth, and the sound in them died away almost at once. Since nothing lingered in the air, players could run through quick notes without everything turning to mush. Then taller halls went up, bare stone all round, and every sound dragged a long tail behind it. The upshot: those same quick notes came out as porridge, so the people writing music slowed down, stretched their chords, preferred held notes to ornament. Later, once such halls had been filled with padded seats and packed audiences, the ringing dropped away again. Writing picked up speed once more, and the pace tightened. Put simply, stone and cloth shaped what went on the page as much as what listeners happened to like.

units: pupils sitting at the back catch only part of the instructions
the cause lies in the surfaces of the room rather than in the speaker
bare walls throw sounds back and the returns run into one another
everybody speaks louder, which raises the noise further still
specialists call this mechanism a spiral
absorbing panels are fitted to the ceiling
pads under the chairs do away with the scraping
the layout of the tables turns voices towards the listeners
teachers strain their voices less once these changes are made
the money spent stays modest
text: In plenty of classrooms, the pupils at the back catch only half of what they are told. The fault seldom lies with the teacher's voice. It lies with the walls. A bare room throws sound back, the returns pile up, and syllables blur into one another. Everybody then speaks a good deal louder, and the level climbs further still. Acousticians call this a spiral of noise. Getting out of it takes very little indeed. Porous panels are fixed to the ceiling to soak up part of what comes back. Felt pads go under the chairs so that they no longer scrape across the floor. Tables are turned about so that every mouth faces a set of ears. Where this has been done, teachers push their voices less and pupils hold on to instructions better. The outlay stays small, and the difference is audible from the first lesson.

units: a neighbour upstairs plays an instrument with plucked strings
a neighbour on the ground floor plays a worn guitar
the narrator likens the two musics to two kinds of rain
the music from above gives separate notes parted by silences
the music from below makes a continuous fabric that cannot be counted
the power fails during a storm
the two neighbours then play at the same time without having arranged it
the narrator listens from the stairwell of the building
the mixture makes a music unlike either of the first two
the neighbours stop playing when the power returns
text: The woman who lives above me plays the harp, and the man on the ground floor scrapes away at a worn guitar. In the end I came to compare their music the way you might compare two kinds of rain. Hers falls in separate drops, each note clean, each parted from the next by a polite silence. His pours in a sheet: strings answer strings, fingers rasp, and nothing can be counted. One stormy evening the power failed across the building, and the two of them began playing at the same moment, without a word between them. From the stairwell I heard the drops land on the sheet. It was neither of the two musics: it was a third, one that neither of them could have written down. When the light came back they stopped, each door closed, and the building went back to being two flats stacked up.

units: the preparation follows three ordered stages
the room holding the most furniture is the one to choose
anything making a background noise has to be switched off
a thick cloth is hung behind whoever is speaking
the microphone goes at chin height and slightly to one side
the tilt keeps the expelled air from striking the diaphragm
the stand belongs on the floor rather than on a piece of furniture
a short stretch of silence is recorded to gauge the background noise
listening is done on headphones and not through a loudspeaker
one complete take is kept before any editing
text: Before you record a voice at home, get the room, the microphone and the session ready, in that order. The room: pick whichever one holds the most furniture, shut the windows, switch off anything that blows or hums, and hang a thick blanket behind you. The microphone: set it at chin height, a hand's width away from the mouth, tilted a little to one side so that the breath of your consonants misses the diaphragm. Stand it on a weighted floor stand, never on the table, since wood carries every knock straight up. The session: record a short stretch of silence first, which gives you a measure of the background. Then speak at a steady level, without drifting nearer or further away. Listen on headphones, never through a loudspeaker. And keep one full spare take before you cut anything at all.

units: work on a concert venue has just come to an end
complaints had been piling up over a whole season
the lower sounds became inaudible from the far rows back
an acoustic survey was commissioned and then passed to those in charge
the decision was taken to clear the vaulted ceiling
the panels that threw the sound back were removed
the armchairs were swapped for seats whose absorption never varies
the stage floor was given a rake
a musical ensemble played without an audience to test the place
those in charge will wait a full season before drawing conclusions
text: Work on the concert hall came to an end last week, closing a project the musicians had followed closely. It had been launched after a full season of complaints: once the ceiling was redone, the lower instruments vanished for anyone sitting in the back rows. An acoustic survey was commissioned and then passed to the management, which decided to open the vaulted ceiling up again. The workers went on to take down the reflecting panels, swap the armchairs for seats whose absorption never varies, and put a rake into the stage floor. A trial orchestra played behind closed doors to measure how the room answered. The readings confirmed a gain in clarity in the lower register. Performances will resume, the management announced, warning that the real verdict cannot come in before a full season of use.

units: the workshop is heard before it is seen
the craftsman strikes a heated piece of metal
each blow makes a short sound that the metal walls throw back
the pitch of the sound shifts because the metal is cooling
the sound grows higher as the material hardens
the sandy floor takes in part of what comes back
a blower keeps the fire going and makes a continuous noise
the ear grows used to that continuous noise and keeps only the blows
the quiet after the stop seems sharper than it really is
text: A forge makes itself heard well before anyone catches sight of it. The smith hammers away at a heated bar, and every blow tears out a short, almost shrill sound that bounces straight back off the metal walls. Because the bar cools as it is struck, the note keeps shifting: it climbs as the metal hardens, and it drops again once the flame has softened the bar. The sandy floor swallows part of what comes back, so the din stays bearable for anyone working in there all day. At the far end, a blower breathes over the embers, and its steady drone sits underneath everything else. Since the ear grows used to that drone, it ends up hearing nothing but the blows. When the hammer stops, the quiet seems far deeper than it truly is, for hearing keeps the trace of the sound just gone a moment longer.

units: the listener does not decide what music is played in public places
the point of playing it is to slow the customers down
the writer locates the problem in the absence of any prior agreement
no way of stopping the playback is offered
those who hear poorly are put out more than the rest
background music covers voices and makes conversation tiring
a first measure is to bring in stretches with nothing playing
these stretches would be announced at the door and would cost nothing
a second measure lowers the volume until talking becomes possible
a third measure hands the setting over to the staff of the place
text: You hardly ever choose the music you hear any more. Step into a shop, a lift, a waiting room, and a tune meets you, pitched to slow your walk along the shelves. The trouble is not taste, it is consent. Nobody ever asked whether you wanted to listen, and nobody offers you any way of stopping it. For those who hear poorly the thing is worse still: the wash of sound covers voices and makes talking exhausting. So what can be done about it? First, make silence available: a stretch with nothing playing at all, announced at the door, costs nothing and would relieve the whole trade. Second, drop the level to the point where two customers can speak without raising their voices. Third, let the staff work the controls, since they are the ones who take the loop from start to finish. None of this needs a law.
